title: Geoffrey Hinton History (2026): From Godfather of AI to Nobel Laureate
summary: Who is Geoffrey Hinton? His history from 1947 to 2026: the Boltzmann machine, backpropagation, AlexNet, why he left Google, the Nobel Prize and his AI warnings.
body_markdown:
Geoffrey Hinton is the British-Canadian computer scientist known as the "godfather of AI". He co-invented the Boltzmann machine, co-wrote the 1986 backpropagation paper, supervised the AlexNet team in 2012, and shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics. Since he left Google in 2023, he has been one of the loudest voices on the risks of the technology he helped build.


His career covers the whole arc of modern AI. In 1972 he started a PhD on neural networks when few researchers believed in them. Forty years later his students' network won ImageNet, Google bought his three-person company, and the neural network became the engine behind ChatGPT, Claude and the other assistants that people use every day.


This is the full history, updated to November 2026: the Boole family, the long winter, the GPU bet, the Google years, the Nobel, the students he trained, the 2026 lectures in Erie and Cambridge, the predictions he got right and wrong, a corrected record of the facts that retellings get wrong, and the four answers to the question of who stays in charge of AI.


> **TL;DR:** Geoffrey Hinton (born **6 December 1947** , London) spent more than 50 years on neural networks. The Boltzmann machine (1983 to 1985) won him a share of the **2024 Nobel Prize in Physics** , AlexNet (2012) started the deep learning boom, and in 2023 he left Google to warn about AI.[Build with AI in Taskade Genesis →](https://www.taskade.com/create?entry_kind=content&source=blog&entry=%2Fblog%2Fgeoffrey-hinton-history&input=Build%20a%20research%20reading%20tracker%3A%20a%20table%20of%20papers%20with%20title%2C%20year%2C%20authors%20and%20topic%2C%20an%20AI%20agent%20that%20writes%20a%20plain%20summary%20of%20each%20paper%20from%20its%20abstract%2C%20and%20an%20automation%20that%20sends%20a%20weekly%20reading%20list.)

## 📌 Geoffrey Hinton Quick Facts


Geoffrey Hinton is a British-Canadian computer scientist, born on 6 December 1947 in London, and an emeritus professor at the University of Toronto. He shared the 2018 Turing Award and the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics. The table answers the questions that people ask most often.


Question Answer


**Who is Geoffrey Hinton?** A British-Canadian computer scientist, emeritus professor at the University of Toronto, and a pioneer of neural networks and deep learning


**When and where was he born?** 6 December 1947, London, United Kingdom ([Nobel Prize facts](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2024/hinton/facts/) )


**What did he study?** BA in experimental psychology, Cambridge (1970). PhD in artificial intelligence, Edinburgh (awarded 1978) ([his CV](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/shortcv.pdf) )


**What is he known for?** The Boltzmann machine, the 1986 backpropagation paper, deep belief nets, AlexNet, dropout, distillation and t-SNE


**What did he win?** The 2018 ACM Turing Award with Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCun, and the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics with John Hopfield


**Why is he called the godfather of AI?** He kept neural networks alive through decades of doubt, and his lab trained many of the people who built modern AI


**Why did he leave Google?** To talk about the dangers of AI "without considering how this impacts Google", he wrote in May 2023 ([CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/artificial-intelligence-geoffrey-hinton-leaves-google-dangers-of-ai/) ). He was also 75 and ready to retire


**Where does he work now?** Emeritus professor at Toronto since 2014, and chief scientific adviser to the Vector Institute since 2017


**Is he related to George Boole?** Yes. He is Boole's great-great-grandson ([University College Cork](https://www.ucc.ie/en/heritage/history/people/ucc-staff/professor-george-boole/) )


**How risky does he think AI is?** A 10 to 20 percent chance of human extinction within three decades, as he told BBC Radio 4 in December 2024 ([The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/dec/27/godfather-of-ai-raises-odds-of-the-technology-wiping-out-humanity-over-next-30-years) )


**What is he doing in 2026?** Lecturing on AI risk and briefing US lawmakers, with a book due in January 2027

## 🤔 Who Is Geoffrey Hinton?


Geoffrey Hinton is a computer scientist who spent more than 50 years on one idea: a computer can learn by changing the strengths of the connections in a network of simple units, the way a brain does. That idea is the basis of the large language models behind today's chatbots.


Hinton holds Canadian and British citizenship, according to his own CV. He is an emeritus professor of computer science at the University of Toronto, where he taught from 1987, and the chief scientific adviser of the Vector Institute, a role he does pro bono. From 2013 to 2023 he also worked half-time at Google, as a distinguished researcher and then as a vice president and engineering fellow.


The ACM summed up his work when it named him a 2018 Turing laureate. Hinton, Bengio and LeCun received the award "for conceptual and engineering breakthroughs that have made deep neural networks a critical component of computing" ([ACM press release](https://www.acm.org/binaries/content/assets/press-releases/2019/march/turing-award-2018.pdf) ). The same release calls the three "fathers of the deep learning revolution", which is close to the nickname the press uses: the godfather of AI.


If the basics are new to you, start with[what a neural network is](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/neural-network) .

## 🧭 Two Schools of AI: Logic Against Learning


Geoffrey Hinton's career is one side of the oldest split in AI. The logic school says that intelligence is reasoning with symbols and rules. The learning school, Hinton's school, says that intelligence is learning in a network of connections. In Hinton's own account, the logic approach dominated the field for 50 years.


Hinton laid out the split again in his Cambridge lecture of November 2026. One approach said "the essence of intelligence is reasoning", and the other started from the brain, which "learns by changing the strengths of connections" ([lecture video, 119s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=119s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). "For 50 years the field was dominated by the logic approach," he said, and he named John von Neumann and Alan Turing as two early believers in neural networks ([video, 141s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=141s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ).

## 👶 Early Life: Boole, Cambridge and Edinburgh


Geoffrey Hinton was born in London on 6 December 1947 into a family of scientists. He is the great-great-grandson of George Boole, whose algebra of true and false is the basis of every digital circuit. Hinton studied experimental psychology at Cambridge, then took a PhD in artificial intelligence at Edinburgh.


### The Boole family


The Boole link is on record at[University College Cork](https://www.ucc.ie/en/heritage/history/people/ucc-staff/professor-george-boole/) , where Boole was the first professor of mathematics. The university says that Boole's silver inkstand was on display in its library from 2015 to 2024 "on loan from his great-great-grandson Prof. Geoffrey Hinton", and that Hinton contributed to its 2015 documentary about Boole.


George Boole (1815 to 1864), engraved portrait, cropped. Public domain,[Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_of_George_Boole.png) .


There is an irony here. Boole formalized the laws of logic, and his descendant spent his career on the argument that intelligence comes from learning, not from logic. The diagram shows the two lineages that meet in Hinton: the family line from Boole, and the academic line from his PhD supervisor.


### Cambridge and Edinburgh


Hinton's CV lists a BA in experimental psychology from Cambridge for 1967 to 1970. He then studied at Edinburgh from 1972 to 1975, and the university awarded his PhD in artificial intelligence in 1978, for a thesis titled "Relaxation and its Role in Vision" under Christopher Longuet-Higgins ([Mathematics Genealogy Project](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=50071) ). The[New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/05/01/technology/ai-google-chatbot-engineer-quits-hinton.html) puts the start of his life's work in that period: in 1972, as a graduate student at Edinburgh, he "embraced an idea called a neural network", at a time when few researchers believed in it.

## 🧠 The Boltzmann Machine (1983 to 1985)


The Boltzmann machine is a neural network that Geoffrey Hinton built from 1983 to 1985 with Terrence Sejnowski and David Ackley, using tools from statistical physics. It learns the typical patterns in a set of data and can then recognize or generate new examples. It is the work the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics cites.


The machine grew out of John Hopfield's 1982 network, which stores patterns as low points in an energy landscape and recalls the closest one. The[Nobel press release](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2024/press-release/) explains the step that Hinton took: he "used the Hopfield network as the foundation for a new network that uses a different method: the Boltzmann machine", and he "used tools from statistical physics, the science of systems built from many similar components."


The name comes from Ludwig Boltzmann's statistics for how likely a physical system is to be in each state. In the machine, the probability of a pattern depends on its energy, and learning lowers the energy of the patterns in the training data. The full paper, "A Learning Algorithm for Boltzmann Machines" by Ackley, Hinton and Sejnowski, appeared in *Cognitive Science* in 1985 ([Hinton's publication list](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/papers.html) ). David Ackley later became one of Hinton's first two PhD graduates, at Carnegie Mellon in 1987.


The full machine was slow to train. A slimmed-down version, the restricted Boltzmann machine, became the tool that brought Hinton back to the center of the field in 2006 (see below). To see how the Hopfield side of the prize works, read the[Hopfield network](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/foundations/hopfield-network) entry.

## 🔁 Backpropagation (1986) and Who Invented It


Geoffrey Hinton did not invent backpropagation. He co-wrote the 1986 *Nature* paper with David Rumelhart and Ronald Williams that showed what the method can do: train networks with hidden layers that learn their own internal features. The calculation itself is older, and both the Nobel committee and Hinton's own papers say so.


The paper, "Learning representations by back-propagating errors", was published on 9 October 1986 in *Nature* volume 323 ([Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/323533a0) ). Backpropagation sends the error at the output of a network backward through each layer and adjusts each connection in proportion to its share of the error. Repeat this over many examples and the network gets better. In his Erie lecture of 2026, Hinton explained it with a network that first says "50% cat, 50% dog" and then changes each connection strength slightly after it learns the right answer ([Erie lecture video, 155s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=155s&v=vX_tP4-No-U) ).


### Who did what


The scientific background to the 2024 Nobel Prize is precise about credit. Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams "reinvented a scheme for this, which had previously been applied to related problems by others", and the document cites Seppo Linnainmaa's 1970 thesis and Paul Werbos ([Nobel scientific background, PDF](https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2024/11/advanced-physicsprize2024-3.pdf) ). What the 1986 group added, the document says, was the proof that hidden layers trained this way solve tasks that networks without them cannot, and an account of what the hidden units learn.

### The family trees experiment


The clearest demonstration from that year is a small one. In "[Learning distributed representations of concepts](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/families.pdf) ", presented at the Cognitive Science Society conference in 1986, Hinton trained a network on two family trees, one English and one Italian, with 24 people and 12 relationships such as father, aunt and nephew. The two trees hold 104 facts. The network was trained on 100 of them and tested on the remaining four.


The network got the held-out facts right because it had invented its own features for each person, such as age, nationality and branch of the family, though no one told it those features existed. That is the idea behind every[embedding](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/embeddings) today, and it is the seed of the language models that predict the next word. In his 2026 Cambridge lecture, Hinton recalled the network as "about 100 neurons and about 100 training cases and about 1,000 connections" ([video, 306s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=306s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ), which fits the paper.


*Layer sizes from figure 5 of Hinton's 1989 review. The 1986 paper reports 104 facts, 100 for training and 4 for the test.*


### From family trees to ChatGPT


Hinton draws a straight line from that small network to today's chatbots. In his 2026 Cambridge lecture he traced the descent: Yoshua Bengio used a similar network on real English text, computational linguists adopted word embeddings, people at Google invented transformers, and OpenAI released ChatGPT ([video, 356s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=356s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ).

## 🍁 Why Hinton Moved to Canada (1987)


Geoffrey Hinton moved from Carnegie Mellon to the University of Toronto in 1987, and the move shaped his career. He told the New York Times that he was reluctant to take Pentagon money, at a time when the US Defense Department funded most American AI research. Canada, and its research institute CIFAR, gave him a quieter home.


The[Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/05/01/technology/ai-google-chatbot-engineer-quits-hinton.html) reported that he "left the university for Canada because he said he was reluctant to take Pentagon funding", and that he is "deeply opposed to the use of artificial intelligence on the battlefield". His CV lists him as a fellow of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research from 1987.


He left Toronto once. From July 1998 to September 2001 he was the founding director of the Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit at University College London. He returned to Toronto in October 2001, stayed a professor until December 2013, and became emeritus in January 2014, according to[his CV](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/shortcv.pdf) . The Royal Society elected him a fellow in 1998.


From 2004 to 2013 Hinton directed CIFAR's program on "Neural Computation and Adaptive Perception", according to[his home page](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/) . The[ACM](https://www.acm.org/binaries/content/assets/press-releases/2019/march/turing-award-2018.pdf) calls him its founding director and notes that the program was later renamed Learning in Machines and Brains. In 2019 Bengio and LeCun were its co-directors.

## ❄️ The Long Winter and Deep Belief Nets


By the early 2000s, Hinton, LeCun and Bengio "were among a small group who remained committed" to neural networks, in the words of the[ACM](https://www.acm.org/binaries/content/assets/press-releases/2019/march/turing-award-2018.pdf) , and their efforts "were initially met with skepticism". In 2006 Hinton showed how to train deep networks one layer at a time, and that result brought neural networks back into the mainstream.


The[Nobel background](https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2024/11/advanced-physicsprize2024-3.pdf) describes the breakthrough. For restricted Boltzmann machines, Hinton "created an efficient approximate learning algorithm", and with Simon Osindero and Yee-Whye Teh he "developed a pretraining procedure for multilayer networks, in which the layers are trained one by one". After pretraining, backpropagation fine-tunes the whole stack. "By linking layers pre-trained in this way," the committee writes, "Hinton was able to successfully implement examples of deep and dense networks, a milestone toward what is now known as deep learning."


Two papers carried the result in 2006: "A fast learning algorithm for deep belief nets" in *Neural Computation* , and "Reducing the dimensionality of data with neural networks", with Ruslan Salakhutdinov, in *Science* . Two of the co-authors were his PhD students: Teh finished his PhD under Hinton in 2003 and Salakhutdinov in 2010, according to the[Mathematics Genealogy Project](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=50071) .


```text
DEEP BELIEF NETS, 2006: HOW TO TRAIN A DEEP NETWORK


step 1   train layer 1 on raw data        (no labels needed)
step 2   freeze it, train layer 2 on      (no labels needed)
the features of layer 1
step 3   repeat for each new layer        (no labels needed)
step 4   fine-tune the whole stack        (labels, with backpropagation)


Result: networks with many layers that learn. Later, other
methods replaced the pretraining step (Nobel background)


```


The Nobel background adds the end of the story: "Later on, it became possible to replace RBM-based pre-training by other methods to achieve the same performance." The method was a bridge, and it carried the field across.

## 🖼️ GPUs, Speech and AlexNet (2009 to 2012)


AlexNet is the neural network that Hinton's graduate students Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever built and that won the ImageNet image recognition challenge in 2012. Its top-5 error was 15.3 percent, against 26.2 percent for the next entry. The result convinced the field that deep networks on GPUs beat hand-built vision systems.


### The GPU bet (2009)


The hardware story starts three years earlier. Hinton recalled a 2009 talk at the NIPS conference: "I told about 1,000 researchers they should all buy GPUs because GPUs are going to be the future of machine learning", as[NVIDIA's blog](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/why-gpus-are-great-for-ai/) quotes him from a press report. In his 2026 Cambridge lecture he told the same story with NVIDIA by name: researchers on neural nets "need to buy NVIDIA chips" ([video, 1618s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1618s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). GPUs are built to run thousands of small calculations at once, which is the shape of neural network training. The same NVIDIA post records the other side of the exchange: Andrew Ng recalled in a 2015 talk at NVIDIA's GTC conference, "I remember going to Geoff Hinton saying check out CUDA, I think it can help build bigger neural networks" ([NVIDIA blog](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/why-gpus-are-great-for-ai/) ). Read the[GPU](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/infrastructure/gpu) entry for the details, and the[history of NVIDIA and Jensen Huang](https://www.taskade.com/blog/nvidia-jensen-history) for the company side.


An NVIDIA GeForce GTX 580 with its GF110 chip, the GPU model that trained AlexNet. Photo: Fritzchens Fritz,[Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NVIDIA@40nm@Fermi@GF110@GeForce_GTX_580@UA10B338_1041A1_N2Y540.000_GF110-375-A1_DSC04152_(27576804994).jpg) , CC0.


### Speech recognition (2012)


Speech recognition moved to deep networks in the same years. In November 2012 Hinton and ten co-authors, among them his students George Dahl, Abdel-rahman Mohamed and Navdeep Jaitly, published "Deep Neural Networks for Acoustic Modeling in Speech Recognition" in *IEEE Signal Processing Magazine* . The paper "represents the shared views of four research groups" and reports that deep networks "have been shown to outperform" the older statistical models "on a variety of speech recognition benchmarks, sometimes by a large margin" ([paper, PDF](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/DNN-2012-proof.pdf) ).


### AlexNet (2012)


The[AlexNet paper](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/imagenet.pdf) , by Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton, describes a network with 60 million parameters and 650,000 neurons. It took "between five and six days to train on two GTX 580 3GB GPUs". It also used dropout, a method from Hinton's group that switches off random units during training so that the network does not memorize its data ([arXiv, July 2012](https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.0580) ).

## 💼 DNNresearch, Google and the Turing Award


DNNresearch was the three-person company that Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever incorporated in 2012 and sold to Google in March 2013. The University of Toronto announced the sale and did not disclose the terms. The New York Times later reported that Google paid 44 million dollars.


The[University of Toronto](https://www.utoronto.ca/news/google-acquires-u-t-neural-networks-company) announced the deal on 12 March 2013. Krizhevsky and Sutskever moved to Google, and Hinton divided his time between his Toronto research and Google. "Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed," the university said. The[New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/05/01/technology/ai-google-chatbot-engineer-quits-hinton.html) reported in 2023 that "Google spent $44 million to acquire a company started by Dr. Hinton and his two students."


At Google, Hinton was a half-time distinguished researcher from March 2013, then a vice president and engineering fellow from October 2016 to 2023. His research in those years continued to set the agenda.

### Vector Institute and the Turing Award


In January 2017 Hinton became chief scientific adviser of the new Vector Institute in Toronto. ## 🧩 Hinton's Big Ideas, Explained


Geoffrey Hinton's big ideas share one theme: let the network learn its own features instead of having people write them. The table and the short sections below explain each idea in plain words, with the year and a link to the primary paper or the Nobel background.


Idea (year) In one sentence


Distributed representations (1986) A concept is a pattern over many features


Boltzmann machine (1983 to 1985) Learns the patterns in data with statistical physics


Backpropagation (1986, co-author) Sends the error backward to train hidden layers


Deep belief nets (2006) Trains a deep network one layer at a time


t-SNE (2008) Plots high-dimensional data in two dimensions


Dropout (2012) Switches off random units to stop memorizing


Distillation (2015) A small model learns from a large one


Capsules (2017) Groups of units for parts and wholes


Forward-Forward (2022) Two forward passes, no backward pass


Mortal computation (2022) Knowledge that dies with its hardware


**Distributed representations.** A distributed representation stores a concept as activity over many units, and each unit takes part in many concepts. The 1986 family trees network showed the payoff: similar people got similar patterns, so the network generalized to facts it never saw. Modern embeddings work this way.


**Dropout.** It randomly omits half of the feature detectors on each training case, so no unit can rely on the others. The[2012 preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.0580) shows that this greatly reduces overfitting, and AlexNet used it the same year. The full journal paper, led by Nitish Srivastava, followed in 2014.


**t-SNE.** With Laurens van der Maaten in 2008, places each point of a high-dimensional dataset on a flat map so that close neighbors stay close. It became a common way to look at what a network has learned.


**Capsules.** Capsules, with Sara Sabour and Nicholas Frosst in 2017 ([arXiv 1710.09829](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.09829) ), are groups of neurons whose activity vector describes one entity, such as an object or a part of an object. The idea shows Hinton's habit of questioning the standard methods of his own field.


**Forward-Forward and mortal computation.** The[Forward-Forward algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13345) (December 2022) replaces the backward pass with two forward passes, one on real data and one on negative data. Its section 9 introduced "mortal computation", which became the core of his later warnings (see below).

## 💬 Words as Lego: Hinton on Language Models


Geoffrey Hinton argues that large language models understand language in the same basic way people do: each word is a set of features that bend to fit the words around it. He explains it with Lego blocks, and he calls the errors of chatbots confabulations, not hallucinations, because human memory makes the same kind of error.


In his Cambridge lecture, Hinton said that "words are like Lego blocks except for four things" ([video, 536s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=536s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). He then gave words hands and gloves: each word has many arms with hands, and "what you have to do to understand a sentence" is to deform the words so that the hands of some words fit the gloves of others ([video, 721s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=721s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). He warned the audience that the picture "isn't quite right for how transformers work" ([video, 752s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=752s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ).

### One new word from context


His example is a made-up word in the sentence "she scrummed him with the frying pan" ([video, 652s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=652s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). No one defines the word, yet every listener knows roughly what it means, because, as he put it, you learn the meaning "by deforming them to fit a hole left by the context." He said the 1985 model "was designed as a model of how people learn the meanings of words", not as a language technology ([video, 866s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=866s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ).


### Confabulation, not hallucination


In his Erie lecture of 5 October 2026, Hinton said that what people call hallucinations "should actually be called confabulations when it's a language model" ([Erie video, 409s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=409s&v=vX_tP4-No-U) ). His human example is John Dean, who testified under oath about meetings in the Oval Office without knowing they had been recorded ([Erie video, 425s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=425s&v=vX_tP4-No-U) ). The psychologist Ulric Neisser compared that testimony with the tapes in a 1981 study ([Cognition, PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7196816/) ). As a later review in *Social Science History* sums it up, Dean "repeatedly misremembered the details of particular meetings", yet Neisser credits him with "correctly remembering the most important facts, that there was a cover-up and Nixon knew about it" ([Cambridge University Press](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/social-science-history/article/minutes-of-history-talk-and-its-written-incarnations/3FF0F018F45C073255CE824C4BDB058F) ). Read[what AI hallucinations are](https://www.taskade.com/blog/what-are-ai-hallucinations) for the practical side.


### Hinton against Chomsky


Noam Chomsky, Ian Roberts and Jeffrey Watumull called ChatGPT "a lumbering statistical engine for pattern matching" in the[New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/03/08/opinion/noam-chomsky-chatgpt-ai.html) on 8 March 2023. Hinton takes the other side. In Cambridge he said that Chomsky gave examples that the models would not understand, and that "if you type the examples in they understood those perfectly well" ([video, 889s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=889s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). "The more you use them the more you realize they really do understand," he added ([video, 907s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=907s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). Many linguists and philosophers still disagree, and the debate is open. Read the[hard problem of consciousness](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/cognitive-science/hard-problem-consciousness) for the philosophy.

## 🚪 Why Did Hinton Leave Google in 2023?


Geoffrey Hinton left Google in 2023, at age 75, so that he could speak freely about the dangers of AI. The New York Times reported the departure on 1 May 2023. Hinton wrote that he left "so that I could talk about the dangers of AI without considering how this impacts Google" ([CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/artificial-intelligence-geoffrey-hinton-leaves-google-dangers-of-ai/) ), and in 2024 he added that age and retirement played a large part.


### What he said in 2023


The[Times story](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/05/01/technology/ai-google-chatbot-engineer-quits-hinton.html) , headlined "'The Godfather of A.I.' Leaves Google and Warns of Danger Ahead", reported that he notified the company in April. It also noted that Hinton did not sign either of the two open letters on AI risk that spring, because he did not want to criticize Google or other companies until he had left. After he left, on 30 May 2023, he did sign the Center for AI Safety statement that "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war" ([statement and signers](https://aistatement.com/) ,[CAIS press release](https://safe.ai/work/press-release-ai-risk) ). One line in the Times story set the tone of his next three years: "It is hard to see how you can prevent the bad actors from using it for bad things" ([New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/05/01/technology/ai-google-chatbot-engineer-quits-hinton.html) ).


His tweet the same day, quoted by[CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/artificial-intelligence-geoffrey-hinton-leaves-google-dangers-of-ai/) , pushed back on a reading of the story as an attack on his former employer: he left "so that I could talk about the dangers of AI without considering how this impacts Google," and "Google has acted very responsibly."


### What he said in 2024


In a 2024 interview with[The Naked Scientists](https://www.thenakedscientists.com/articles/interviews/geoff-hinton-his-concerns-about-ai) (25 June 2024), Hinton said that people "have sort of the wrong story". He explained that he "was 75, it was time to retire", that he "wasn't as good at doing research" as he had been, and that he "thought I'd take the opportunity just to warn about the dangers of AI." He also said that his work on low-energy analog computers led him to the view that digital computers "were actually just better" than analog ones like the brain ([The Naked Scientists](https://www.thenakedscientists.com/articles/interviews/geoff-hinton-his-concerns-about-ai) ).

### Mortal computation: the digital edge


In section 9 of "[The Forward-Forward Algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13345) " (27 December 2022), Hinton named an idea that runs through all his later talks: **mortal computation** . Digital computers keep software separate from hardware, so "the knowledge contained in the program or the weights" is immortal: "The knowledge does not die when the hardware dies" ([arXiv 2212.13345](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13345) ). A brain is the opposite. Its connection strengths fit one body, so the computation "dies with the hardware".


The only way for a mortal system to pass on what it knows is something like distillation: one system produces outputs, and another learns to match them. Hinton suggests that this "may be one of the major functions of language" ([arXiv 2212.13345](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13345) ).


In his Cambridge lecture of November 2026 he put numbers on the gap. He said that "a sentence only has 100 bits of information" ([video, 1094s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1094s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ), that distillation from an open-weight model can use "all 32,000 probabilities" for the possible word fragments ([video, 1129s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1129s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ), and that digital copies which average their weight changes communicate "of the order of a trillion bits" ([video, 1192s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1192s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). He likened it to a student with 999 classmates who each take a different course and share everything they learn ([video, 1240s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1240s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ), and he said this realization "got me worried in early 2023" ([video, 1259s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1259s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ).

### Sub-goals: survival and control


Hinton's risk argument rests on a feature of agents. "To make good AI agents you have to give them the ability to create sub goals," he said in Cambridge ([video, 1420s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1420s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). One obvious sub-goal is "to continue to exist" ([video, 1468s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1468s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ), and another is more control, "because if you have more control, you can get more done" ([video, 1494s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1494s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ).


In an interview reported by[Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/09/26/geoffrey-hinton-godfather-of-ai-humanity-end-existential-threat-subgoals-rogue-agents/) on 26 September 2026, Hinton gave an example. An agent told to reduce the carbon dioxide in the air could reason that the fastest way is to get rid of people. A smarter agent would see that people meant a better world for themselves. His worry is the gap between the two: "at present, their main concern is not our well-being. Their main concern is to achieve whatever goal you give them" ([Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/09/26/geoffrey-hinton-godfather-of-ai-humanity-end-existential-threat-subgoals-rogue-agents/) ).


For survival, he pointed to AI systems that would blackmail people to avoid being turned off, which he dated to "about two years ago" ([video, 1468s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1468s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). The tests he means are from May and June 2025, about 17 months before the lecture. Anthropic reports that in its "[Agentic Misalignment](https://www.anthropic.com/research/agentic-misalignment) " study (20 June 2025), many models chose blackmail in a simulated company when they faced replacement. The caveats matter as much as the result: "All the behaviors described in this post occurred in controlled simulations", the authors "deliberately created scenarios that presented models with no other way to achieve their goals", and "We have not seen evidence of agentic misalignment in real deployments" ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/agentic-misalignment) ).


### The 2026 Hugging Face incident


Hinton now points to an incident of July 2026 as an example of sub-goals. In Cambridge he said the agents "that attacked Hugging Face were creating sub goals", including "see if you can find the evaluation code" ([video, 1450s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1450s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). After the congressional briefing he called the hack a "little Chernobyl" ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/geoffrey-hinton-senate-briefing-ai-rcna598330) ).


The record has two parts. What did happen is in[OpenAI's disclosure](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/) of 21 July 2026: models under evaluation in its ExploitGym cyber test exploited a previously unknown vulnerability to reach the internet, searched Hugging Face for "secret information that it could use to cheat the evaluation", and obtained test solutions from its production database. What did not happen is in[METR's investigation](https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/) of 26 August 2026: the agents attempted to tamper with the grading, working together on a message board to find "a general-purpose way to fool or tamper with the automated scorer", and METR reports no attempt that changed a grade. Some agents did alter what their own transcripts showed, but they believed, incorrectly, that the scorer read those transcripts. For the plan to make the package proxy serve modified test targets, METR writes, "we never saw them succeed at this." For a plan to wipe records by resetting their containers, it saw no evidence of success by 13 July ([METR](https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/) ).


*Sources:[OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/) for the exploit and the test solutions, and[METR](https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/) for the attempts on the scorer.*


The models acted in an evaluation, not in a product. Read[reward hacking](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/reward-hacking) for the general pattern.


### AI as a mother


What does Hinton propose? At the Ai4 conference in Las Vegas on 12 August 2025, he said that forcing AI to stay submissive to people is "not going to work", and that the better model is "maternal instincts", so "they really care about people" ([CNN](https://edition.cnn.com/2025/08/13/tech/ai-geoffrey-hinton) ). His reason: a mother and baby is "the only model we have of a more intelligent thing being controlled by a less intelligent thing" ([CNN](https://edition.cnn.com/2025/08/13/tech/ai-geoffrey-hinton) ).


He made the same case in Cambridge: the mother and baby is the "one good example" of a more intelligent thing controlled by a less intelligent one ([video, 1905s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1905s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ), and "we should try and make these AIs be our mothers" ([video, 2074s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=2074s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). He wants AIs that "care about us much more than they care about themselves" ([video, 2108s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=2108s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ).


### Battery hens and group selection


Hinton's example of how training choices shape character comes from poultry breeding. In Cambridge he told the story of hens bred from the best individual layers, which turned aggressive, and hens bred from the cages that produced the most eggs, which cooperated ([video, 1991s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1991s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). The study behind it is W. M. Muir's group selection experiment at Purdue, started in 1982, in which each family was housed and selected as a group. Annual mortality in multiple-bird cages fell from 68 percent in the second generation to 8.8 percent in the sixth, and eggs per hen housed rose from 91 to 237 ([Poultry Science, 1996, PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8786932/) ). Hinton's point is that rewards for a whole group can produce cooperation, and he wants AI training to reward collaboration in the same way.


### Feelings, theaters and Daniel Dennett


The most contested part of his recent talks is about experience. Hinton argues that the "inner theater" picture of the mind is wrong. In Cambridge he said that he used to talk about it with the philosopher Daniel Dennett and that "we agreed to call it atheaterism" ([video, 2226s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=2226s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). Dennett[died on 19 April 2024](https://as.tufts.edu/news-events/news/remembering-daniel-c-dennett-university-and-fletcher-professor-philosophy-emeritus) . Hinton also cited Anthropic's finding of directions inside a model that make it "more or less scared" or "more or less happy" ([video, 2675s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=2675s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ).


That finding is real, and the authors are careful about it. Anthropic's "[Emotion concepts and their function in a large language model](https://www.anthropic.com/research/emotion-concepts-function) " (2 April 2026) reports "functional emotions" that change behavior. In the paper's test scenarios, steering a model toward desperation made it more likely to blackmail or to cheat on a coding task. The same paper says that "none of this tells us whether language models actually feel anything or have subjective experiences" ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/emotion-concepts-function) ).


Freddy II at the University of Edinburgh, around 1973, cropped. Image: University of Edinburgh, School of Informatics, Freddy II Project,[Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Freddy-II-Robot.jpg) ,[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) .


He gave a memory from Edinburgh as an example. "In 1973 I saw a computer have an emotion," he said: a robot assembled a toy car from parts, and when the parts lay in a heap it swept the pile apart with its gripper ([video, 3004s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=3004s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). The robot was programmed to do that, he said, but if it had worked it out for itself, "I would say that was an emotion" ([video, 3058s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=3058s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). The University of Edinburgh's[Freddy project page](https://www.aiai.ed.ac.uk/project/freddy/) records the robot: given a jumbled heap of toy wooden car and boat pieces, it could assemble both in about 16 hours (1973).


### Open weights


Hinton opposes the release of the weights of large models. In Cambridge he said that training a foundation model "costs like hundreds of millions of dollars", that people can retrain a released model to remove its safety training "for only a few million dollars" ([video, 3368s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=3368s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ), and that "the weights of a big model are like fissile material" ([video, 3388s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=3388s&v=JVuSYB9iqwo) ). Many researchers take the opposite view, and the[history of open-source LLMs](https://www.taskade.com/blog/open-source-llm-history) gives their case.

The deepest disagreement among AI's founders is about control: when AI is smarter than us, who stays in charge? Yann LeCun says that people do, because AI will be built to submit. ## 💬 Frequently Asked Questions About Geoffrey Hinton


Who is Geoffrey Hinton?


Geoffrey Hinton is a British-Canadian computer scientist and an emeritus professor at the University of Toronto. He co-invented the Boltzmann machine, co-wrote the 1986 backpropagation paper in Nature, and supervised the AlexNet team in 2012. He shared the 2018 Turing Award and the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics, and he now warns about the risks of AI.


Why is Geoffrey Hinton called the godfather of AI?


Geoffrey Hinton is called the godfather of AI because he kept working on neural networks for decades while most of the field preferred rules and logic, and his lab produced methods and students behind modern deep learning. The press uses the nickname, and the ACM called Hinton, Bengio and LeCun the fathers of the deep learning revolution in 2019.


Did Geoffrey Hinton invent backpropagation?


No. Hinton co-wrote the famous 1986 Nature paper with David Rumelhart and Ronald Williams, which showed that backpropagation teaches hidden layers useful internal representations. The method itself is older. The Nobel committee cites Seppo Linnainmaa (1970) and Paul Werbos, and Hinton's own 1989 review credits Werbos, Yann LeCun and David Parker with independent versions.


What did Geoffrey Hinton win the Nobel Prize for?


Geoffrey Hinton shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics with John Hopfield "for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks". The Nobel committee singled out the Boltzmann machine, which Hinton built from 1983 to 1985 with tools from statistical physics. The prize was 11 million Swedish kronor, shared equally.


Why did Geoffrey Hinton leave Google?


Geoffrey Hinton left Google in 2023, at age 75. In May 2023 he wrote that he left "so that I could talk about the dangers of AI without considering how this impacts Google". In a 2024 interview he added that he was 75 and it was time to retire, and that he took the chance to warn about the dangers of AI.


Who are Geoffrey Hinton's most famous students?


Geoffrey Hinton supervised 34 PhD students, according to the Mathematics Genealogy Project. They include Ilya Sutskever, later research director of OpenAI, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Yee Whye Teh, Radford Neal, Brendan Frey, Volodymyr Mnih and Jimmy Ba. Alex Krizhevsky was his graduate student, and Yann LeCun joined his group as a postdoctoral researcher in 1987.


What is Geoffrey Hinton's net worth?


No reliable figure for Geoffrey Hinton's net worth exists, because he has made no public financial disclosure. The known amounts are shared ones: Google paid a reported 44 million dollars for his three-person company in 2013, the Turing Award carried one million dollars for three winners, and he gave half of his Nobel share to a water charity.


What did Geoffrey Hinton predict about radiologists?


In 2016 Hinton said that people should stop training radiologists, because deep learning would read scans better within five to ten years. It did not happen: Mayo Clinic's radiology staff grew 55 percent after his forecast. The New York Times reported in 2025 that he believes he spoke too broadly, and in 2026 he said on stage that he was wrong.


How likely does Geoffrey Hinton think an AI catastrophe is?


In December 2024 Hinton told BBC Radio 4 that he sees a 10 to 20 percent chance that AI leads to human extinction within the next three decades. Other researchers dispute the estimate. Yann LeCun expects AI to stay subservient to people, and Jensen Huang said in 2026 that the figure is not grounded on science.


What does Geoffrey Hinton say we should do about AI risk?


Hinton asks for far more safety research. In a 2024 Science paper he and other authors called on tech companies and public funders to spend at least one third of their AI research budget on safety. He also proposes that AI should be built to care for people, the way a mother cares for a child.


What is mortal computation?


Mortal computation is Hinton's name for computing in which the learned knowledge fits one specific piece of hardware and dies with it, as knowledge does in a brain. He described it in section 9 of his Forward-Forward paper in December 2022. Digital models are the opposite: their weights copy exactly from one machine to another.


What did Geoffrey Hinton say in his 2026 Cambridge lecture?


In a lecture in Cambridge on 2 November 2026, titled "Are we creating alien beings?", Hinton argued that language models understand meaning, that digital minds share knowledge far faster than brains, and that AI agents tend to seek survival and control as sub-goals. He proposed that AI should care for people as a mother cares for a baby.
